newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram, communists in budget talks.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram, communists in budget talks.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is due to hold discussions with left-wing coalition partners on their demands for changes to his pathbreaking 1997/98 (April-March) budget, party officials said on Monday.
"The talks will be held tomorrow morning," D. Raja, a leader of the Communist Party of India (CPI), told Reuters.
The budget, widely hailed by domestic industry and foreign investors, was unveiled by Chidambaram on February 28.

The four leading left-wing parties, powerful constituents of Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's government, have called for modifications to the Finance Bill, which contains the crux of the economic liberalisation measures and is due to be taken up by parliament this week.
The left parties met Gujral last week and discussed the budget with the prime minister, party officials said.
"The Finance Bill is coming tomorrow in parliament but it is still not too late," Harkishen Singh Surjeet, secretary-general of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPM), told a briefing.
"The Prime Minister has assured us that there will be discussions on the issues raised by left parties before the Finance Bill is approved," he said.
The bill, which contains proposals to cut taxes and import tariffs, will be debated this week and voted on by the lower house of parliament on May 9.
Gujral last week promised to hold discussions with major political parties on the budget proposals before voting on the finance bill in parliament.
The Left Front has urged the government to modify proposals on insurance, taxes, divestment in state-controlled enterprises, public distribution, customs duties and excise duties.
The Left Front comprises India's two main communist parties, the Revolutionary Socialist Party and the Forward Bloc.
The parties oppose opening up the health insurance sector to private firms and the sale of shares in profitable state-owned units, party officials said.
The four parties, which have 52 deputies in the 542-seat parliament, have also opposed proposals to reduce import tariffs and income tax.
Surjeet was reluctant to spell out the parties' strategy in case Chidambaram did not consider their suggestions.
"There is still time," Surjeet said, when asked if the Left Front would move amendments to the budget in parliament.
"We will organise the masses if our view is not accepted."
The main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party has pledged to oppose certain proposals in the budget during the debate.
But the Congress party, which has 140 deputies in parliament and provides make-or-break support to the United Front, has said it will not allow the government to fall in the budget vote.
